title: RBAC, OWASP basics and LLM risks
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Role and permission checks (@PreAuthorize, FastAPI dependencies), SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, CORS and secrets handling, and LLM risks: prompt injection and cross-tenant leaks.
source: OWASP Top 10 and Cheat Sheet Series; OWASP API Security Top 10; OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications; Spring Security reference; FastAPI docs; Oracle JDBC docs

questions.prompt: Annotate a Spring service method Order getOrder(String ownerId, long id) so it runs only for users with the ADMIN role or when ownerId equals the authenticated user's name. Write the annotation line.
questions.explanation: hasRole adds the ROLE_ prefix, so hasRole('ADMIN') matches the authority ROLE_ADMIN. The annotation only works when @EnableMethodSecurity is present and the bean is called through its Spring proxy, so self-invocation bypasses it.

questions.prompt: Write a FastAPI dependency factory require_role(role) that depends on get_current_user, raises HTTPException 403 when role is not in user.roles, and otherwise returns the user.
questions.explanation: Use it as @router.delete("/x", dependencies=[Depends(require_role("admin"))]). A closure-returning dependency is the idiom; a class with __call__ is an alternative.

questions.prompt: Match each access-control model to its defining idea.

right.text: Permissions are granted to roles, and users hold roles
Decisions evaluate attributes of user, resource and context
Each object carries a list of who may do what
Access follows relationships in a graph, such as owner or member of
Access is granted by network location only

questions.explanation: Real systems combine them: roles for coarse access, attributes or ownership checks for fine access (the ownerId == name check above is attribute-style).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Authorisation must be enforced on the server even when the UI hides forbidden buttons.
questions.reason: Broken access control was ranked first in the OWASP Top 10 (2021 edition).

whys.a: The ranking is true but it is not why server-side checks are needed.
whys.b: Right: both are true; the real cause is that clients are untrusted, which the ranking merely reflects.

questions.explanation: Hiding UI is usability; checking on the server is security. Missing object-level checks (BOLA) lead the OWASP API Security list too.

questions.prompt: This code is injectable: String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"; Statement st = conn.createStatement(); ResultSet rs = st.executeQuery(sql); Rewrite it with a PreparedStatement and a bound parameter.

checks.label: binds the value with a setter

questions.explanation: Parameters travel separately from the SQL text, so data can never change the query structure. Table and column names cannot be bound; allowlist them. JPA named parameters and Spring JdbcTemplate placeholders do the same.

questions.prompt: Using the Python DB-API with sqlite3 (cursor cur), run the query SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = <email> safely with the variable email and assign cur.fetchone() to row.
questions.model:
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?", (email,))
row = cur.fetchone()
questions.explanation: The one-element tuple needs the trailing comma. psycopg and mysql drivers use %s, sqlite3 uses ?. Never use f-strings to build SQL.

questions.prompt: The users table has 7 rows. Code builds "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'" and the attacker sends the input x' OR '1'='1. How many rows come back?
questions.explanation: The query becomes WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1', and the OR condition is true for every row, so all 7 return. The same trick with UNION or stacked statements can read other tables.

questions.prompt: bcrypt's cost factor is a work exponent. How many key-expansion rounds does cost factor 12 perform?
questions.explanation: The work is 2^cost, so 2^12 = 4096. Each +1 doubles the time, which lets you tune hashing speed as hardware improves.

questions.prompt: Which measures help against CSRF for a cookie-authenticated web app? Select all that apply.

options.text: SameSite=Lax or Strict on the session cookie
options.why: Right: the browser withholds the cookie on cross-site requests.

options.text: A synchroniser or double-submit CSRF token on state-changing requests
options.why: Right: the attacker's page cannot read the token.

options.text: Checking Origin or Referer on unsafe methods
options.why: Right: a defence in depth check.
CORS relaxes the browser's read restrictions, it is not a CSRF defence.

questions.explanation: Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default for browser flows; stateless bearer-token APIs often disable it deliberately.

questions.prompt: A stateless API that authenticates only with an Authorization: Bearer header (never cookies) is not vulnerable to classic CSRF.

options.why: Right: browsers do not attach an Authorization header automatically on cross-site requests.
Cookies are attached automatically, bearer headers are not, so the CSRF mechanism has nothing to ride on.

questions.explanation: The caveat: if the token is kept in a cookie, or XSS can read it, other attacks remain.

questions.prompt: Configuring CORS on the server stops other sites and tools such as curl from calling the API.

options.why: CORS does not authenticate or block callers.
Right: CORS is enforced by browsers to control which origins may read responses; curl ignores it, so you still need authentication.

questions.explanation: In FastAPI, CORSMiddleware with an explicit allow_origins list is correct; avoid allow_origins=["*"] together with credentials.

questions.prompt: Match defence to attack by filling the blanks.
questions.text: Stop XSS with output {1} and a Content-Security-Policy, stop SQL injection with {2} queries, and stop CSRF with SameSite cookies and anti-forgery {3}.
questions.explanation: Defences are specific: encoding fits XSS, parameters fit SQLi, tokens fit CSRF.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Blocking the phrase "ignore previous instructions" fully prevents prompt injection.
questions.reason: Attackers can paraphrase, translate or encode their instructions.

whys.d: Right: the assertion is false because keyword filters are easily evaded, and the reason says why.

questions.explanation: Treat model output and tool arguments as untrusted, limit the tools the agent can reach, and require confirmation for risky actions.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: In a multi-tenant RAG app the tenant filter must be applied inside the vector search query.
questions.reason: If the system prompt says "only reveal data for tenant A", the model will reliably refuse to expose other tenants' documents.

whys.c: Right: prompts are not an access control; the filter belongs in retrieval code.

questions.explanation: Enforce isolation before text enters the context: tenant id filter or separate namespace per tenant, then check document ACLs.

questions.prompt: Which controls prevent cross-tenant data leaks in an LLM feature? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apply the tenant id as a mandatory filter or namespace in retrieval
options.why: Right: nothing from another tenant can reach the prompt.

options.text: Include the tenant id in semantic-cache keys
options.why: Right: otherwise tenant A's cached answer can be served to B.

options.text: Check each retrieved document against the caller's permissions
options.why: Right: filters can be misconfigured; this is the second lock.

options.text: Tell the model in the prompt not to mention other tenants
options.why: A prompt is advice, not enforcement.

questions.explanation: Defence in depth: isolate at retrieval, cache and logging layers; never rely on the model to police access.
